chunks: Al-Sakuni narrated from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from his forefathers, from ʿAlī عليه السلام:
He عليه السلام was asked about a man who saw a bird and followed it until it landed on a tree. Then another man came and took it, so he said:
"What the eye saw belongs to the eye, and what the hand took belongs to the hand."

key_terms.أَبْصَرَ: saw or spotted with the eye
key_terms.أَخَذَتْ: took or seized, indicating actual possession
key_terms.السَّكُونِيُّ: Al-Sakuni, the narrator transmitting this hadith
key_terms.شَجَرَةٍ: a tree on which the bird landed
key_terms.طَيْرًا: a bird being pursued and then taken
key_terms.لِلْعَيْنِ: for the eye; referring to mere sight without possession
key_terms.لِلْيَدِ: for the hand; referring to actual taking or possession

ai.seo_question: Does merely spotting an animal make it yours in Islamic law, or does ownership require actually taking it?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a dispute over possession by distinguishing between mere sight and actual taking. It indicates that simply seeing or pursuing something does not establish ownership, whereas possession is tied to actual seizure in this context.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.3431 - Al-Sakuni narrated from Imam Jafar ibn Muhammad Al-Sadiq (as) from his father, Imam Muhammad ibn Ali Al-Baqir (as), from his forefathers, from Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (as):
He (as) was asked about a man who saw a bird and followed it until it landed on a tree. Then another man came and took it.
Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (as) said: "What the eye sees belongs to it, and what the hand takes belongs to it."
